summary: This informational document is a roadmap to RFCs relating to TCP. It briefly summarizes the documents defining TCP and its extensions, as a guide for implementers and others.

eli5.summary: TCP has many rulebooks. This RFC is a map that tells you which book to read for each topic.

questions: what are the core tcp rfcs
subtitle: A guide to which RFCs define TCP, which extend it, and which ended up on the shelf.

tldr.problem: TCP is specified by many documents spread over decades, mixing standards, experiments, advice and abandoned ideas, so newcomers and implementers do not know which ones matter.
tldr.mechanism: The roadmap sorts TCP-related RFCs into groups (core, strongly encouraged, experimental, historic, support documents) and gives each a short description and a category letter.
tldr.outcome: It is Informational and descriptive only, not a standard. It obsoletes RFC 4614 and has been updated by RFC 7805.

sections.title: Purpose and How to Read the Roadmap
sections.content:
This roadmap organizes the TCP-related RFCs for newcomers and for old hands. It is explicitly not an update of RFC 1122 and not a rigorous standard for what must be implemented. Its categorizations are not definitive, and its content alone should not drive implementation decisions.

A letter after each RFC number gives its category: S Standards Track, E Experimental, I Informational, H Historic, B Best Current Practice and U Unknown. The category does not always reflect relevance. For example, RFC 5681 is part of the required core even though it is only a Draft Standard. Documents flagged '(Errata)' have known technical errors reported after publication. Within each section, entries run in the order of publication.

The three main sections are broadly like MUST, SHOULD and MAY, though the authors stress that the document is merely descriptive.
sections.eli5: This is the table of contents for a huge shelf of TCP books. Each entry has a letter that says whether the book is an official rule, an experiment, a note, or an old idea.

sections.title: Core Functionality
sections.content:
A small group of documents define what must be followed for interoperability: header parsing, the state machine, congestion control and retransmission timeout computation. RFC 793 is the fundamental specification. The roadmap notes its section 3.6, on IP precedence and security compartment, is mostly irrelevant today, and that it has no congestion control; otherwise most of it still describes modern TCPs.

The other core entries are RFC 1122, an Applicability Statement that fixes bugs in RFC 793, RFC 2460 for the IPv6 pseudo-header, RFC 2873 which removes IPv4 precedence processing, RFC 5681 for congestion control (slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit and fast recovery, together called Reno), RFC 6093 on the urgent mechanism, RFC 6298 for the retransmission timer, and RFC 6691 on the MSS option. RFC 6298 changes the initial RTO from 3s to 1s.
sections.eli5: These are the few books everyone has to follow so two computers can understand each other: how the envelope is laid out, how a conversation starts and ends, and how to slow down when the road is crowded.

sections.title: Strongly Encouraged Enhancements
sections.content:
This section lists recommended changes that improve performance and security. It is grouped by topic: fundamental changes such as RFC 7323 (window scaling, timestamps and protection against wrapped sequence numbers), congestion control additions such as ECN (RFC 3168) and a larger initial window (RFC 3390), and loss recovery such as selective acknowledgment (RFC 2018) and NewReno (RFC 6582).

Other groups cover detecting spurious retransmissions (DSACK, Eifel, F-RTO), Path MTU Discovery (RFC 1191, RFC 1981 and RFC 4821), header compression (RFC 1144 and RFC 6846) and defenses against spoofing and flooding. The last group includes the TCP Authentication Option (RFC 5925), which obsoletes the TCP MD5 Signature option of RFC 2385, and RFC 6528 on sequence number attacks. RFC 7323 and RFC 2018 are examples of how much of this is described as commonly found in current systems.
sections.eli5: These extra books are not strictly required, but they make TCP faster, tougher against bad guys, and better at recovering when packets get lost.

sections.title: Experimental Extensions
sections.content:
Experimental RFCs, and some Proposed Standards that are not widely deployed, are listed here. Experimentation is encouraged, but there is not yet formal consensus that they are fully logical and safe, so wide deployment should be well thought out.

Examples include TCP Fast Open (RFC 7413), which allows data in the SYN and SYN-ACK packets and saves up to one round trip compared with the three-way handshake, RFC 6928 which proposes an initial window of 10 segments, and the Multipath TCP documents RFC 6356 and RFC 6824. Experiments that need a new TCP option code point should follow RFC 6994, and RFC 4727 reserves options 253 and 254 for experimentation.
sections.eli5: These are new ideas being tried out. They look promising, but people want more testing before calling them official.

sections.title: Historic and Undeployed Extensions
sections.content:
Some extensions failed to attract implementers or were found defective. Most were reclassified as Historic by RFC 6247. Examples are the TCP Big Window and Nak options (RFC 1106, found defective, and RFC 1110), T/TCP (RFC 1644, found defective and prone to denial-of-service attacks), and TCP Cookie Transactions (RFC 6013), placed here because the authors know of no wide deployment and it uses experimental option code points.

The roadmap notes that one idea from T/TCP, sharing state across connections, lives on in RFC 2140. The RFC also covers support documents (foundational works, architecture, difficult network environments, tools and MIB modules), IANA parameter procedures, and a few undocumented features, namely header prediction, FACK and congestion control for high rate flows. It states that it introduces no new security considerations.
sections.eli5: Some ideas were tried and put back on the shelf because nobody used them or they had problems. The map still lists them so you know they exist.
